extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and archivists interested in U.S. federal government data, web policy, and censorship events
extracted.subtask_description: A factual encyclopedic summary of the 2025 removals and modifications of U.S. federal government web pages and datasets, including background legal/policy context, affected agencies, examples of removed content, legal responses, and preservation efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPEN Government Data Act (2019) data-sharing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The OPEN Government Data Act ordered agencies to share data that could be used to evaluate the effectiveness of their programs and to guide policymaking; various federal agencies release data on their own websites and Data.gov was established to improve public access to high-value, machine-readable datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background: Data.gov (established 2009) and the 2019 OPEN Government Data Act are cited as the statutory and policy framework promoting public access to federal datasets; removal or deletion of datasets runs counter to these statutory aims and impacts civic technology, research, and business applications that rely on government data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act established a system for utilizing data to construct evidence-based policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the second Trump administration's actions as a dramatic pivot away from the law's intent, implying that agency data stewardship and availability are expected under this Act and that large-scale deletions undermine evidence-based policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 'Defending Women' compliance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: On January 29, 2025 the Office of Personnel Management ordered agencies to comply with President Trump's executive order 'Defending Women,' which requires federal agencies to 'recognize women are biologically female, and men are biologically male'. Organizations were told to terminate any programs and remove any outward facing media, documents, materials, communications, and statements that promote 'gender ideology' by January 31.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: agencies were given rapid deadlines to remove or modify content that could be construed as promoting 'gender ideology,' leading to removal or stripping of terminology on many web pages; this is an explicit, time-bound administrative directive constraining agency web content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 'Ending Radical Government DEI Programs' prohibition on terms and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies were instructed to comply with an executive order banning 'radical' DEI programs and to remove forbidden terms from their websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and effects: many pages had DEI-related terms removed or replaced (e.g., 'climate change' → 'climate resilience', 'LGBTQ' → 'LGB', 'pregnant people' → 'pregnant women'); the directive functioned as a content-control standard enforced across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data Use Agreements and HIPAA constraints on external archiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Many datasets cannot be archived by outside researchers because they are regulated by Data Use Agreements that must be consistent with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: even when researchers or archivists attempt to mirror or preserve federal data, DUAs and HIPAA create legal/technical limits on what can be copied or redistributed, complicating rescue and preservation efforts described in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional mandate under the Global Change Research Act (National Climate Assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Climate Assessment reports are congressionally mandated under the Global Change Research Act of 1990.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance: taking mandated reports or the teams that produce them offline (e.g., dismissing staff, removing assessments) implicates statutory obligations and raises questions about compliance with congressional mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency change-management and approval standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to official agency web content are expected to follow internal approval and leadership processes; the National Park Service stated changes to the Underground Railroad page were made 'without approval from NPS leadership nor Department leadership'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: the article treats unauthorized or unapproved edits as a deviation from expected change-management norms, highlighting that web revisions should be authorized to ensure accuracy and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal remedies and judicial intervention for removals
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal responses can require restoration: lawsuits were filed (e.g., Doctors for America) and a federal judge issued a restraining order on February 11, 2025 requiring certain HHS, CDC, and FDA websites to be restored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the article documents that removals can be challenged in court and that courts may grant injunctive relief when plaintiffs argue removals harm public health, research access, or violate law/policy; litigation is a formal mechanism to contest administrative deletions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and archiving best-practices and initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple organizations and initiatives (Internet Archive, End of Term Web Archive, Harvard Law School Library's Data.gov Archive, IPUMS, Data Rescue Project, PEGI, Library Innovation Lab) undertook efforts to mirror, copy, and preserve deleted government datasets and pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Internet Archive archived many datasets and the End of Term Web Archive attempts to copy government publications at administration transitions; the article suggests coordinated preservation is a recommended countermeasure when official data are at risk of deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory context for specific content (e.g., DOJ databases, reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain government datasets and pages are tied to statutory or regulatory functions (e.g., DOJ charge records, National Institute of Justice studies, congressionally mandated reports) which bear on whether removal is legally permissible or compliant with recordkeeping obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites debates over whether particular deletions (e.g., January 6 charges database) may violate law and notes that removal of statutory/regulatory material can prompt legal and policy scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational directives for internal access and data destruction (HHS DOGE memo example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal directives asserted that DOGE employees had 'full access to all unclassified agency records and software and IT systems' and were tasked with obligations including 'destroy or erase copied HHS data or information when no longer needed for official purposes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates administrative rules controlling internal access and lifecycle of copied data, signaling operational constraints on how employees and contractors must handle data subject to review or deletion.
